faq.q: What is it like to live in Halkidiki all year round?
faq.a: Calm and practical, if you choose the right place. The coast is lively in summer and quiet in winter. Towns with a permanent population, such as Nea Moudania, Polygyros and Ierissos, keep shops, schools and services open all year, and Thessaloniki is close enough for shopping, hospitals and flights.

faq.q: Can I retire to Greece from the UK?
faq.a: Yes. UK citizens can retire to Greece, but since Brexit they are non-EU and need a residence permit to stay longer than 90 days in any 180-day period. As of November 2026, common routes include a permit for people with independent income, such as a pension, and the Golden Visa. Our lawyer can confirm which fits you.

faq.q: Which are the best beaches in Halkidiki?
faq.a: It depends on your taste. Kassandra has long sandy, organised beaches. Sithonia is known for clear coves and pine forest, especially around Vourvourou and in the south of the peninsula. Aristotelis has the long beach of Ierissos and quiet coves towards Ouranoupoli. Try several before choosing where to buy.

faq.q: Is healthcare available in Halkidiki for foreign residents?
faq.a: Yes. There is a general hospital in Polygyros, health centres in larger towns and pharmacies in most villages, with the large hospitals of Thessaloniki within reach. Foreign residents usually need private health insurance or registration with the Greek system, depending on their residence status. Check your own situation before you move.

faq.q: Is Halkidiki a good place to retire?
faq.a: For many people, yes: a slower pace, the sea, long summers and a major city close by. Choose a town with year-round services, check access to healthcare and plan your residence permit and taxes in advance. Spending a winter here before buying is a good test.

intro: Halkidiki beaches are what first bring most people here: clear water, pine trees down to the sand and three peninsulas to explore. Many visitors come back year after year, and some decide to move to Greece for good. This guide covers the beaches, everyday life through the seasons, retiring, healthcare and getting around, so you can see which part of Halkidiki, in Northern Greece, suits you.
body:
Halkidiki's best beaches by peninsula

Every part of Halkidiki has good beaches, and each peninsula has its own character.

  • Kassandra has long sandy beaches on both coasts, many organised with sunbeds and beach bars. The west coast is known for its sunsets, the east coast for its lively resorts.
  • Sithonia has smaller coves, clear water and pine forest, from the shallow bays around Vourvourou on the east coast to the beaches south of Neos Marmaras and around Sarti. Many are quieter and less developed.
  • Aristotelis has the long beach of Ierissos and quiet coves towards Ouranoupoli, with views of Mount Athos.
  • Nea Propontida and the coast of Polygyros have long, easy beaches close to year-round towns, popular with families.

Which are the best beaches in Halkidiki depends on what you want: organised and lively, or quiet and wild. If you are thinking of buying, spend a day on the beaches near each home you view, both on a weekday and at a weekend.

The swimming season usually runs from late spring into early autumn, and September is a favourite month for many residents: the water is still warm and the beaches are much quieter. Outside summer, the same beaches are perfect for long walks.

Beyond the sand, the coast offers boat trips, sailing, diving and fishing, and the forests behind the beaches have walking and cycling routes for the cooler months.

Living in Halkidiki all year round

Summer and winter are two different worlds. From late spring to early autumn the coast is busy, restaurants are full and visitors fill the resorts. In winter many resort villages become very quiet, with only a few shops and tavernas open.

If you plan to live here all year, choose a place with a permanent population. Nea Moudania, Polygyros, Kassandreia, Nikiti and Ierissos are examples of towns and villages with schools, shops, banks and services that stay open. Check heating and insulation in any home you consider, as winter evenings can be cool and damp.

Many residents enjoy the contrast: a lively summer, then calm months with empty beaches, walks in the forest and village life. Thessaloniki is close enough for shopping, culture and flights.

Daily life is simple and local. Most towns have supermarkets, bakeries and a weekly open-air market with fruit, vegetables and fish from the area. Learning some Greek makes a real difference, especially with neighbours and public offices, although English is widely understood in the resort areas.

Retiring to Greece from the UK or USA

Halkidiki attracts retirees who want the sea, a slower pace and access to a city. EU citizens can live in Greece and register their residence. Since Brexit, UK citizens, like US citizens, are non-EU and need a residence permit to stay longer than 90 days in any 180-day period.

As of November 2026, to be confirmed by our lawyer, the main routes for non-EU retirees are a permit for people with sufficient independent income, such as a pension, and the Golden Visa through property. Each has its own conditions on income, health insurance and documents. Tax residence is a separate question, so speak to an accountant about pensions and tax before you move.

We help with the property side: finding a home that fits a retired life, with shops, health services and the sea within easy reach, and ideally on one level or with few stairs.

On the practical side, every new resident needs a Greek tax number (AFM) and usually a Greek bank account, and non-EU citizens need their residence permit before staying beyond the visa-free limit. A local lawyer and accountant can handle most of the paperwork, and much of it can start before you move.

Not every retiree moves full time. Many spend the long season in Halkidiki and the coldest months at home, near family. If that is your plan, choose a home that is easy to close up and look after from a distance; we offer property management for owners who are away.

Healthcare and services

Halkidiki has a general hospital in Polygyros, the regional capital, and health centres in larger towns such as Nea Moudania, plus pharmacies in every larger village. For specialist care, the large hospitals of Thessaloniki are within reach by road. Private doctors and clinics also work in the area.

Foreign residents usually need private health insurance or must register with the Greek public system, depending on their status. Banks, supermarkets, post offices and public services are found in the larger towns all year.

In an emergency, the European number 112 works throughout Greece. Pharmacies take turns to stay open at night and at weekends, and the pharmacist is often the first stop for minor health questions. If you have a long-term condition, check in advance which specialists you will need and where they are.

Getting around: Thessaloniki airport and roads

Thessaloniki airport is about one hour by car from the start of the Kassandra peninsula, with flights to many European cities, some of them only in summer. Nea Propontida is a little closer, while Sithonia and Aristotelis take longer.

A car is almost essential. Buses link the main towns with Thessaloniki, but service is limited in the smaller villages, especially in winter. The main roads are good, while some coastal and hillside roads are narrow or unpaved, so check the access to any home before you buy.

Thessaloniki itself is a lively city with a large university, hospitals, shopping centres, a busy cultural life and rail and bus links to the rest of Greece and the Balkans. For many residents of Halkidiki, a day in the city is a regular part of life.

Which area of Halkidiki suits you?

  • Kassandra: convenience, sandy beaches, services and the shortest drive from the airport.
  • Sithonia: nature, quiet coves and privacy.
  • Nea Propontida: year-round town life close to Thessaloniki.
  • Aristotelis: a local, less touristy life near Mount Athos.
  • Polygyros: the regional capital, its services and the coast nearby.

The best way to decide is to visit more than one area, ideally both in and out of season. Many future residents spend a few weeks in the area before buying, to test the drive to the shops, the winter atmosphere and the distance to healthcare. It is time well spent before such an important decision. When you are ready, browse our listings and book a viewing in person or by video.
